design: Cross-country panel combining peering port pricing with proprietary IP-transit pricing data, 2019-2024
title: Dissecting the cost of peering: Global evidence from internet exchange points (IXPs)
data: Publicly available peering port pricing combined with proprietary IP-transit pricing data
findings: Peering costs are substantially lower than IP-transit costs across the global sample. Larger cost savings from peering relative to transit are associated with lower broadband prices for consumers, expanded mobile network coverage, and higher overall telecommunications revenues. These associations are most pronounced in moderately regulated economies and in low- and lower-middle-income countries.
magnitude: Peering-vs-transit cost savings are linked to lower broadband prices, with the strongest effects in low- and lower-middle-income countries

design: Instrumental variables using historical Eisenhower interstate highway corridors (which fiber-optic routes tend to follow) to instrument for data-center capacity siting, state-level…
authors: Asa Watten, John Bistline, Geoffrey Blanford
title: Have Data Centers Raised Your Electric Bill? Causal Evidence from the United States
data: State-level panel of data center capacity and residential electricity prices, 2015-2024
findings: Using an IV strategy that isolates data-center siting from unobserved local price drivers, a doubling of data-center capacity is found to causally lower residential electricity prices by about 3.5% at a fixed level of demand. The typical residential customer lived in a state where data-center capacity grew 160% between 2019 and 2024, which is estimated to have cut their electricity rates by about 6%. The results reject the hypothesis that data centers shift costs onto residential ratepayers while capturing discounted industrial rates.
magnitude: A doubling of data center capacity causally lowers residential electricity rates by about 3.5%, rejecting a cost-shifting-to-households narrative

design: Ring comparisons around 1,118 geocoded facilities using satellite night-lights, plus a built-versus-announced-but-cancelled near-miss design (43 built vs 49 cancelled hyperscale si…
title: The local economic impact of data centers
data: 1,118 geocoded data-center facilities (341 hyperscale), VIIRS satellite night-time radiance, advertised-salary and new-firm registration panels, school district finance records, residential electricity prices
findings: A carefully designed null result, and a useful corrective to industry impact studies. The physical footprint of a data center is unmistakable — night-time radiance within 1km of an isolated site jumps 38-70 percent at construction start, fading to near zero beyond 5km. But the local economic spillovers are not detectable: advertised salaries and new-firm registrations show no significant increase, with 95 percent confidence intervals ruling out increases above 5.5 percent and 1.6 percent respectively. Rents rise modestly (2-5 percent in synthetic control). School district property-tax revenue rises 16.6 percent and capital outlay per pupil 28.5 percent, but neither survives correction for multiple testing across six fiscal outcomes, and the authors describe them as suggestive rather than robust. Residential electricity prices show no increase. Notably, the paper tests a shift-share instrument similar to that used elsewhere in this literature and rejects it, finding it independently predicts manufacturing and health-sector activity and so violates the exclusion restriction.
magnitude: Capital footprint +38-70% at the parcel, but no detectable wage or firm-entry effect (95% CI upper bounds 5.5% and 1.6%)

design: Formalized 'Water and AI Feedback Loop' framework with a constructed Water Consumption Impact index measuring community-level utility burden at ten data center sites
authors: Basit A. Akinade, Amobichukwu C. Amanambu, Jonathan M. Frame, Shaolei Ren
title: AI Data Centers and the Water Use Feedback Loop
data: Water withdrawal/consumption and utility capacity data for ten US data center sites
findings: The authors formalize how AI data-center water use for cooling, local water scarcity, and AI-driven efficiency tools interact in a feedback loop, and construct a Water Consumption Impact index to measure the burden data centers place on host community water systems. Across ten US sites examined, this burden ranges from just 0.2% to as much as 134% of host community water capacity, a three-order-of-magnitude spread showing that water stress from data centers depends overwhelmingly on local siting and infrastructure rather than facility size alone.
magnitude: Data-center water withdrawal ranges from 0.2% to 134% of host community water capacity across ten US sites studied

design: Game-theoretic model of data-center operator renewable-certificate/PPA choices plus difference-in-differences using staggered large-language-model releases as natural experiments o…
authors: Dana Golden, Aruna Balasubramanian, Niranjan Balasubramanian
title: Certificates without Electrons? Theory and Evidence on Impacts from AI-Driven Power Demand
data: Novel dataset linking AI model release activity to local grid outcomes (wholesale prices, outage frequency) in PJM zones
findings: Data centers represent about 4.4% of US electricity demand. Using staggered large-language-model releases as natural experiments, wholesale electricity prices rise by up to 25% in treated PJM zones, and outage frequency increases by 0.5-1 additional outages per year near data centers, with impacts scaling with model size. A 'timing wedge' between real-time consumption and annually-averaged renewable energy certificate (REC) attribution means data centers claiming 100% annual REC coverage still degrade grid reliability; behind-the-meter colocation with storage is more effective than RECs alone at mitigating these externalities.
magnitude: Wholesale electricity prices rise up to 25% in PJM zones exposed to data-center load following major AI model releases

design: LLM-based textual analysis of corporate/policy/media disclosures combined with energy-system modeling to project data center electricity footprints and regional grid stress
authors: Danbo Chen, Zijun Zhou, Yongyang Cai, Jiahong Qin, Ani Katchova, Lei Chen
title: Concentrated siting of AI data centers drives regional power-system stress under rising global compute demand
countries: United States, Ireland, Japan, and other major AI-compute hubs
data: Corporate disclosure text analysis (LLM-based) combined with quantitative energy-system modeling for six leading AI firms
findings: More than 90% of projected global AI compute capacity concentrates in North America, Western Europe, and Asia-Pacific. Electricity consumption of six leading AI firms' data centers is projected to rise from about 118 TWh in 2024 to 239-295 TWh by 2030 (roughly 1% of global power demand). A constructed Power Stress Index exceeds critical thresholds (0.25) in Oregon, Virginia, and Ireland, indicating local grid vulnerability, while Texas and Japan show better absorption capacity due to more diversified infrastructure.
magnitude: Six leading AI firms' data center electricity use is projected to roughly double to triple, from 118 TWh (2024) to 239-295 TWh (2030)

design: Difference-in-differences with staggered adoption timing across US data center facility openings
title: The Local Economic Effects of Data Center Entry
venue: SSRN working paper (abbreviated as 'The Local Economic Effects of AI Data Center Entry,' Academy of Management Proceedings, 2026)
data: Staggered-adoption panel of US data center facility openings matched to county economic outcomes (employment, wages, establishments, household income, building permits)
findings: Data center activation increases local employment by 3.5%, total wages by 5.0%, business establishments by 4.7%, and median household income by 1.9%, alongside reduced unemployment and increased building permits. Effects are substantially stronger in metropolitan counties (driven by agglomeration economies) and minimal in non-metro counties; Big Tech-owned facilities generate larger local benefits than third-party data centers, and clustered entries amplify gains. The authors also note potential electricity cost increases for local ratepayers in some areas.
magnitude: Data center entry raises local employment by 3.5% and wages by 5.0%, but effects are concentrated almost entirely in metropolitan counties

design: Shift-share IV (fiber-node proximity x Chinese data-center revenue growth; 1980 urban college population share x rest-of-world data-center revenue growth), county-level long differ…
authors: Fernando E. Alvarez, David Argente, Joyce Chow, Diana Van Patten
title: Data Centers and Local Economies in the Age of AI: A Shift-Share Approach
data: 451 Research Datacenter Knowledge Base (12,960+ facilities, 2,700+ providers, 131 countries) matched to County Business Patterns, IRS Statistics of Income, FHFA house price index, and EIA Form 861 electricity prices
findings: A one-log-point increase in cumulative data-center revenue in a county raises total employment by 3.9%, data-processing employment by 29.4%, establishments by 6.2%, house prices by 17.7%, and electricity prices by 0.9% by 2020 (all significant at 1%); tax returns, adjusted gross income, and wages also rise (5.9%, 8.2%, and 5.9% respectively), though annual payroll responds less robustly. First-stage F-statistics range from 786 to 907. The employment and electricity-price effects weaken and lose significance once state fixed effects are added.
magnitude: Data center revenue growth raises county electricity prices by 0.9% and house prices by 17.7%, with total employment up 3.9% (2SLS, 2020 horizon)

design: Tracking and tabulation of state/local subsidy deals and official tax-exemption fiscal notes across major US data center projects
title: Money Lost to the Cloud: How Data Centers Benefit from State and Local Government Subsidies
period: recent state fiscal years through FY2026
data: State/local economic-development subsidy deal tracking and official state fiscal-note projections of sales-tax-exemption revenue losses
findings: The 11 largest publicly disclosed data-center subsidy megadeals average $1.95 million in public subsidy per permanent job created (e.g., Apple's North Carolina deal is $321 million in incentives for 50 permanent jobs, or $6.4 million per job). At least 10 states are each losing more than $100 million per year to data-center sales/use-tax exemptions: Texas's losses are projected to exceed $1 billion in FY2026 (about $9 billion cumulatively 2025-2030), Virginia's FY2025 cost was about $1.94 billion, Ohio's 2025 cost was about $1.6 billion, and Georgia's FY2026 projection was revised up 664% to $2.5 billion.
magnitude: Major US data center subsidy deals average $1.95 million in public subsidy per permanent job created

design: Event-study analysis using unemployment insurance records, LinkedIn cohort tracking, and syllabus text analysis
authors: Morgan R. Frank, Alireza Javadian Sabet, Lisa Simon, Sarah H. Bana, Renzhe Yu
title: AI-Exposed Jobs Deteriorated Before ChatGPT
data: Monthly US unemployment insurance records by occupation/location; millions of LinkedIn profiles tracking graduate hiring cohorts; millions of university syllabi records measuring curricular AI exposure
findings: Unemployment risk in AI-exposed occupations began rising in early 2022, months before ChatGPT's November 2022 release, and new-graduate cohorts from 2021 onward entered AI-exposed jobs at lower rates than earlier cohorts, with the gap opening before ChatGPT. After ChatGPT's release, graduates with more AI-relevant coursework experienced higher first-job pay and shorter job searches, suggesting curricular AI exposure became an asset even as occupational AI exposure became a risk.
magnitude: AI-exposed occupations' unemployment risk began rising in early 2022, predating ChatGPT's launch by roughly nine months

design: Facility-level emissions accounting combined with the AP4 integrated assessment model and EPA social cost of carbon
title: Measuring the Impact of Data Centers in the United States Economy: Monetary Damage from Air Pollution and Greenhouse Gas Emissions
data: Facility-level data for approximately 2,800 US data centers combined with electricity grid emissions data, the AP4 integrated assessment model, and the social cost of carbon
findings: This paper quantifies the environmental externalities associated with electricity consumption by data centers in the United States, focusing on damages from local air pollution and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Using facility-level data for approximately 2,800 operational data centers in 2025, combined with electricity grid characteristics and emissions data, the analysis estimates pollution impacts through the AP4 integrated assessment model and applies the social cost of carbon for GHG valuation. Results indicate that data centers consume roughly 250 TWh of electricity—about 5–6% of U.S. generation—and generate approximately $25 billion in gross external damages (GED), with a range of $10–$33 billion. These damages are highly geographically concentrated, with Texas and Virginia accounting for 30% of the national total. While GED comprises about 5% of industry GDP, this ratio varies widely across states, exceeding GDP in some regions. Planned data center expansion could increase electricity demand and associated damages by up to 85% in the near term. Despite these environmental costs, preliminary comparisons suggest that the damages attributable to AI-related energy use are small relative to potential productivity gains.
magnitude: US data centers caused about $25 billion per year in gross external pollution and climate damages in 2025

design: Regional wholesale electricity market analysis of data-center load impacts with projections under high-utilization construction scenarios
authors: Owen Kay, Robert Reaser, Reid Taylor
title: Processing Power: The Effect of Data Centers on Wholesale Electricity Markets
venue: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas Working Paper 2606
data: Regional wholesale electricity market price data linked to data center corridors
findings: Existing data centers have already raised wholesale electricity prices by an estimated 2-6% nationwide, with larger effects concentrated in regions hosting major data center corridors. Under high-utilization scenarios with proposed construction continuing, the authors project wholesale prices could rise by as much as 50% through 2028.
magnitude: Data centers have already raised nationwide wholesale electricity prices by 2-6%, with a projected rise of up to 50% by 2028 under high-growth scenarios

design: Input-output economic contribution modelling commissioned by an industry trade association
authors: PwC for the Data Center Coalition
title: Economic contributions of data centers in the United States
data: Industry financial data and employment statistics run through an input-output contribution model, national and state level
findings: The most widely cited industry estimate of the data-center sector's economic footprint, and a useful contrast with the quasi-experimental local studies in this repository. It reports a contribution of $926.9 billion to US GDP in 2024, 5.5 million jobs supported, and $204.4 billion in federal, state and local tax revenue, up from $727 billion and 4.7 million jobs on 2023 data. These are gross contribution figures from an input-output model commissioned by the industry, not causal estimates: they count activity associated with the sector rather than activity that would not have occurred otherwise, and they should not be compared like-for-like with the near-zero local spillovers that credible quasi-experimental designs recover.
magnitude: $926.9 billion gross GDP contribution and 5.5 million jobs supported in 2024 — a contribution accounting figure, not a causal estimate

findings: Estimate the impact of Value Added Tax exemptions on smartphone penetration in Colombia using the synthetic control method. Colombia announced a VAT exemption on low-cost mobile handsets in late 2016 and implemented the change in 2017. The study finds that smartphone penetration rates rose to 66.8 % by the end of 2021, an increase of 7.6 percentage points and +12.8 % over the 59.2 % level of its synthetic counterpart. Additionally, a preliminary cost-benefit analysis suggests that the broader economic gains from increased smartphone penetration could plausibly offset the VAT revenue losses over time.

design: Financial-economics analysis of data center capital structures, financing vehicles, and systemic-risk exposures
title: Financing the AI Buildout
data: Analysis of hyperscaler capex and project-finance/REIT/private-credit deal structures for data centers
findings: The AI data center buildout is estimated to require investment averaging roughly 2.8% of GDP over the 2025-2032 period, a pace comparable to or exceeding the 19th-century railroad investment boom at its peak. Financing is shifting from on-balance-sheet corporate capex toward leases, project finance, securitization, and private-credit/SPV structures, which expand debt capacity but concentrate risk through tenant dependence, technology obsolescence, and circular credit linkages among hyperscalers, chipmakers, and lenders.
magnitude: AI data center buildout investment is projected to average about 2.8% of US GDP through 2032, rivaling the railroad boom at its peak

design: Difference-in-differences on linked survey and matched employer-employee administrative data
title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI (previously circulated as 'Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects')
venue: NBER Working Paper 33777 / Becker Friedman Institute Working Paper
data: Two large-scale AI-chatbot adoption surveys (late 2023 and 2024) covering 25,000 workers and 7,000 workplaces in 11 exposed occupations, linked to Danish matched employer-employee administrative data
findings: Despite near-universal employer adoption of chatbot initiatives in exposed occupations, the study finds precisely estimated null effects of AI chatbots on earnings and recorded hours at both worker and workplace level, ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT's release. Estimated time savings from chatbot use are only about 3%. Null results are robust across intensive users, early adopters, high-investment workplaces, and early-career jobs; employers instead absorbed AI through task reorganization rather than pay or hours changes.
magnitude: Earnings/hours effects ruled out above 2%; time savings ~3%, two years post-ChatGPT

design: High-frequency administrative payroll panel, difference-in-differences controlling for firm-level shocks
authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, Ruyu Chen
title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab / SIEPR Working Paper
data: Monthly administrative payroll records from ADP, the largest US payroll-software provider, by detailed occupation
findings: Early-career workers (ages 22-25) in the most AI-exposed occupations experienced a 16% relative decline in employment since generative AI's widespread adoption, controlling for firm-level shocks, while employment for more experienced workers in the same occupations held stable or grew. Adjustment occurred mainly through headcount rather than compensation, and declines concentrated in occupations where AI automates rather than augments tasks.
magnitude: 16% relative employment decline for 22-25 year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations

design: Randomized field experiment with three arms (no AI / GPT-4 / GPT-4 plus prompt training)
authors: Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Edward McFowland III, Ethan Mollick, Hila Lifshitz-Assaf, Katherine Kellogg, Saran Rajendran, Lisa…
title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
data: 758 BCG consultants (~7% of individual-contributor consultants) randomized across AI-access conditions on a realistic consulting task battery
findings: Inside the 'jagged frontier' of tasks AI handles well, consultants using GPT-4 completed 12.2% more tasks, worked 25.1% faster, and were rated 33.9% higher quality by human graders than the control group. Outside the frontier, on tasks beyond AI's current capability, AI users were 19% less likely to produce correct solutions, and elite consultants using AI produced less varied (more homogeneous) outputs.
magnitude: Inside frontier: +12.2% tasks completed, 25.1% faster, quality +33.9%; outside frontier: -19% correct-solution rate

design: Global energy-demand modeling and industry capex tracking
title: Energy and AI (with 2026 update: data centre electricity use surged in 2025 despite grid bottlenecks)
data: IEA global modeling of data center electricity demand and capex tracking of major technology/cloud firms
findings: Global data center electricity consumption reached about 415 TWh in 2024 (about 1.5% of global electricity use); electricity demand from data centers rose a further 17% in 2025, with AI-focused facilities growing even faster, far outpacing 3% overall global electricity demand growth. Data center consumption is projected to double by 2030, with AI-focused data center power use roughly tripling. Combined capex of five large technology companies surged past $400 billion in 2025 and is set to rise a further 75% in 2026, while about 20% of planned data center projects are at risk of delay due to grid constraints.
magnitude: IEA projects global data center electricity demand will double by 2030, with AI-focused demand roughly tripling

design: Panel of high-frequency CPU utilization data with a structural learning model of within-firm productivity dynamics after cloud adoption
authors: James M. Brand, Mert Demirer, Connor Finucane, Avner Kreps
title: Firm Productivity and Learning with Digital Technologies: Evidence from Cloud Computing
region: not specified (large cloud provider's client base)
data: High-frequency CPU utilization data for nearly 100,000 firms using cloud infrastructure
findings: Firms improve cloud computing productivity by 33% in the first year after adoption and reach a stable productivity level only after four years. Faster learning among initially less-efficient firms narrows productivity dispersion across firms by 60% over time, though substantial heterogeneity persists even after ten years. Productivity gains occur mainly within individual divisions of a firm, with minimal knowledge transfer across divisions of the same firm.
magnitude: Firms raise cloud computing productivity by 33% in their first year of adoption, taking up to 4 years to fully stabilize

design: Randomized controlled trial administering exam questions to law students with/without GPT-4
title: AI Assistance in Legal Analysis: An Empirical Study
data: RCT administering law school exam questions (multiple-choice and essay) to law students randomized to GPT-4 access or no AI access
findings: GPT-4 assistance significantly improved student performance on simple multiple-choice legal questions but did not significantly improve performance on complex essay questions requiring integrative legal reasoning, suggesting current-generation LLMs complement rather than replace higher-order legal analytical skills. This is among the first RCTs isolating AI's causal effect on human legal-reasoning tasks.
magnitude: Significant gains on multiple-choice legal questions; no significant gain on complex essay/legal-reasoning questions

findings: Klaus Deininger et al. (2025) explore how digital technologies can improve the efficiency and inclusiveness of property registries. The study introduces a framework to assess digital registry services across three dimensions: digital coverage, interoperability, and the integration of property taxation for local service delivery and public land management. Analyzing data from 85 countries, the paper reveals significant disparities in digital registry adoption and performance. While some nations have made substantial progress in digitizing property records and enhancing interoperability between agencies, others lag due to infrastructural, legal, or institutional challenges. The authors advocate for strategic reforms that expand digital coverage and promote regular data collection to monitor progress. By strengthening property rights through digital registries, states can bolster public sector efficiency, support equitable economic growth, and foster a more livable environment.

design: Privacy-preserving classification of millions of real AI conversations mapped to O*NET occupational tasks
authors: Kunal Handa, Alex Tamkin, Miles McCain, Saffron Huang, Esin Durmus, Sarah Heck, Jared Mueller, Jerry Hong, Stuart Ritchi…
title: Which Economic Tasks are Performed with AI? Evidence from Millions of Claude Conversations
data: Over 4 million Claude.ai conversations classified by task and occupation via Anthropic's privacy-preserving Clio pipeline, mapped to the O*NET database
findings: Usage concentrates heavily in software development and writing tasks; about 36% of occupations use Claude for at least a quarter of their associated tasks, concentrated in mid-to-high-wage computer and mathematical occupations. Of classified task-level usage, 57% reflects augmentation (iterative collaboration, learning) while 43% reflects automation (directive requests with minimal human involvement).
magnitude: 57% of Claude usage is augmentation vs 43% automation; 36% of occupations use AI for ≥25% of their tasks

findings: Evaluate the impact of integrating Aadhaar-based biometric authentication into India’s Public Distribution System (PDS), which provides subsidized food to over 800 million low-income individuals. Drawing on large-scale randomized controlled trials and administrative data, the study finds that biometric authentication reduced leakages by 11 percentage points - a 41% decline from baseline diversion levels - indicating improved public sector efficiency and targeting accuracy. However, this gain came with significant costs: authentication errors and poor transition management led to exclusion rates of 2–4%, translating to approximately 1.5 to 2 million legitimate beneficiaries facing interruptions in access. These exclusions were largely driven by technological failures, such as connectivity issues and biometric mismatches. The authors emphasize that while digital ID systems can strengthen delivery by reducing fraud, careful attention to infrastructure readiness, user experience, and institutional safeguards is essential to avoid harming the very populations these systems are meant to serve.

design: Refined exposure index combining primary survey, expert Delphi review, and AI-based scoring
authors: Pawel Gmyrek, Janine Berg, Karol Kamiński, Filip Konopczyński, Agnieszka Ładna, Balint Nafradi, Konrad Rosłaniec, Marek…
title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure
data: 29,753 tasks rated by 1,640 employees across ISCO-08 occupational groups; 52,558 task-level automation-potential data points for 2,861 tasks; Delphi expert panels; AI-based scoring; four-tier exposure gradient
findings: Globally, one in four workers (25%) are in occupations with some generative AI exposure, though only 3.3% of global employment falls in the highest-exposure category. Exposure is highly unequal by income level (34% of employment exposed in high-income countries vs 11% in low-income countries) and by gender, with the gap widening as countries get richer: 9.6% of female employment vs 3.5% of male employment is in the highest-exposure category in high-income countries.
magnitude: High-income country exposure 34% vs low-income 11%; female highest-exposure share 9.6% vs male 3.5% in high-income countries

design: Randomized field experiment varying disclosure of AI-based job matching
authors: Sarah H. Bana, Kevin J. Boudreau
title: AI-Enabled Job Markets & Market Participation: A Field Experiment on How AI Shapes Jobseekers' Expectations of Competition
venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab Working Paper
countries: Online job-matching platform (country not specified in available summary)
data: Field experiment with 4,562 jobseekers on an online job-matching platform, randomized across AI-matching disclosure, human-matching, and control conditions
findings: Jobseeker participation was about one-quarter lower when AI-based matching was disclosed compared to a human-matching treatment or an undisclosed control condition. The effect was strongest among jobseekers with STEM backgrounds (greater AI familiarity) and appears driven by beliefs about match quality, what inputs AI uses, and the scale of competition faced, rather than simple AI aversion.
magnitude: ~25% lower jobseeker participation when AI-based matching was disclosed vs. human-matching/control

design: Instrumental variables using zipcode-level timing and speed of high-speed fiber broadband rollout to instrument for cloud adoption, UK firm panel
authors: Timothy DeStefano, Richard Kneller, Jonathan Timmis
title: Cloud Computing and Firm Growth
venue: Review of Economics and Statistics, Vol. 107(6)
data: UK firm-level administrative panel data combined with zipcode-level fiber broadband rollout timing and speed instruments
findings: Cloud adoption increases employment, revenue, and productivity growth for young firms, but their activity becomes concentrated in fewer establishments. For incumbent firms, cloud adoption produces smaller scale effects and weaker productivity gains, and instead drives restructuring through more establishment deaths and fewer births; both young and incumbent firms disperse their remaining establishments farther from headquarters after adopting cloud.
magnitude: Cloud computing raises employment and productivity growth for young firms while triggering establishment closures and geographic dispersion for incumbents

design: County-level logit entry model with Heckman two-stage selection correction on local demand, operating-cost, and fixed-cost shifters
title: Where the Cloud Rests: The Economic Geography of Data Centers
venue: Strategy Science (Harvard Business School Working Paper 21-042)
data: Census of 1,433 US data centers (1,386 third-party facilities scraped from Baxtel.com/Datacenters.com plus facilities of the 4 largest cloud providers) matched to county-level demand, cost, and tax-incentive variables
findings: Third-party data centers show a strong urban bias: 96.4% of counties hosting one are in Metropolitan Statistical Areas, and a one-standard-deviation increase in population density raises entry likelihood by 7.4 percentage points, while a similar increase in local information-sector employment share raises it by 1.9 points. Hyperscale cloud providers follow the opposite logic: only 73% of their host counties are in MSAs, and cloud entry is significantly more sensitive to input costs (higher industrial electricity prices discourage cloud-provider entry, odds ratio 0.40) than to local demand. Fixed costs of entry are about 24% higher in the most competitive (largest) markets.
magnitude: Third-party data centers cluster in cities (96.4% in MSAs) while hyperscale cloud data centers locate based on electricity costs, not local demand

design: US Census Bureau plant-level panel comparing survival/productivity effects of IT-as-a-service (cloud) spending versus owned IT capital investment
title: Economies Before Scale: IT Strategy and Performance Dynamics of Young U.S. Businesses
data: US Census Bureau confidential plant-level microdata, manufacturing sector
findings: Young manufacturing plants that rent IT as a service (cloud) show significantly higher survival rates and growth than those relying on traditional owned IT capital, which instead is associated with a higher likelihood of failure among young plants. Conditional on survival, young plants exhibit substantially higher productivity from IT services expenditure than older incumbent plants, with the effect concentrated in IT-intensive and high-demand-variance industries; young plants also gain productivity from owned IT capital under certain conditions.
magnitude: Renting IT as a service (cloud) raises young manufacturing plants' survival odds, while traditional IT capital investment raises their failure risk

findings: Data centers are the physical infrastructure behind cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and enterprise software. The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) is intensifying demand for compute, accelerating investment in data centers, and raising concerns about the local economic and environmental footprint of these facilities. Their expansion creates a local policy tradeoff. A data center can bring capital investment, construction activity, and specialized employment, but it can also increase demand for electricity, land, and grid capacity. This paper studies these effects at the U.S. county level. We assemble a facility-level panel of global data centers with precise coordinates, scale metrics, and annualized revenue. We map facilities to U.S. counties and combine them with County Business Patterns, county-level IRS income, county-level house prices, and electricity prices. To address endogenous siting, we instrument for data center growth using two shift-share instruments, which leverage pre-existing proximity to InterTubes long-haul fiber nodes and the 1980 county share of U.S. urban college population as shares, and both Chinese and rest-of the- world data center revenue growth as shifts.

design: Harmonized household/labor-force survey analysis combined with task-exposure scoring
authors: World Bank Group, International Labour Organization
title: Buffer or Bottleneck? Employment Exposure to Generative AI and the Digital Divide in Latin America (Quantifying the Jobs Potential of AI in Latin America and the Caribbean)
venue: World Bank / ILO joint policy report
data: Harmonized household and labor-force surveys across LAC countries combined with task-exposure scoring, adjusted for slower technology-adoption speeds in developing economies
findings: 30-40% of jobs in Latin America and the Caribbean are exposed in some way to generative AI, but only 2-5% are at risk of automation, while 8-12% could see productivity gains. Women workers are twice as likely as men to be in jobs at risk of automation, and up to half of exposed workers (about 17 million jobs) lack the digital infrastructure needed to benefit; exposed jobs are disproportionately held by younger, educated, urban workers.
magnitude: 30-40% of LAC jobs exposed to generative AI; only 2-5% at automation risk; women 2x more likely to face automation risk

design: Three encouragement-design field experiments with randomized Copilot adoption incentives
authors: Zheyuan (Kevin) Cui, Mert Demirer, Sonia Jaffe, Leon Musolff, Sida Peng, Tobias Salz
title: The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers
countries: United States and multinational (Microsoft, Accenture, Fortune 100 firm)
data: Randomized encouragement to adopt GitHub Copilot among 4,867 developers across three firms (Microsoft: 1,663; Accenture: 311; Fortune 100 company: 3,054)
findings: Pooling data across all three firms and 4,867 developers, Copilot access increased completed tasks by 26.08% (SE 10.3%). Less-experienced developers adopted the tool at higher rates and realized larger productivity gains than more senior developers, consistent with AI substituting for missing experience.
magnitude: 26.1% increase in completed tasks pooling three field experiments (4,867 developers)

findings: Show that the improvement in information dissemination due to the introduction of 4G leads to an increase in productivity, fertilizer consumption, and credit uptake. The identification strategy exploiting the staggered state-level introduction of Rights of Way (RoW) policies meant to promote the growth of telecom infrastructure echoes similar results. The paper finds that six years after the introduction of 4G internet, the annual income of agricultural households grew by 14.5%. Using detailed farmer-level internet-browsing data, the paper shows that the introduction of 4G is related to internet adoption and acquiring agri-related information.

Employed a theoretical macroeconomic multi-sector model to analyze the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) on sectoral and aggregate employment, output, and inflation. Using an industry exposure index, they found that AI adoption significantly increases output, consumption, and investment in both the short and long run. If AI's productivity boost is unanticipated, it initially leads to disinflation, which later turns into moderate inflation through increased demand. Conversely, if AI's productivity boost is anticipated, inflation rises immediately. The theoretical model underscores that AI's impact on output is twice as large when it affects sectors producing consumption goods rather than investment goods.

authors: Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David J. Deming
title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI
data: First nationally representative US survey (ages 18-64) on generative AI use at work and at home
findings: Found that 32 percent of men use generative AI at work, compared with just 23 percent of women. GenAI usage declines with age, from about 34 percent for workers under age 40 to 17 percent for workers age 50 or above. About 40 percent of workers with a bachelor’s degree or more use generative AI at work, compared with about 20 percent for those without a college degree. 46 percent of workers who majored in science, technology, engineering, or mathematics (STEM) use generative AI at work, compared with 40 percent for workers who majored in business, economics, or communication and 22 percent for all other majors, including liberal arts and humanities.
magnitude: 39.4% adult adoption by August 2024; time savings equivalent to 1.4% of total work hours

design: Large-scale worker survey linked to matched employer-employee administrative registers
title: The Adoption of ChatGPT (published as 'The Unequal Adoption of ChatGPT Exacerbates Existing Inequalities Among Workers')
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS); SSRN/NBER Summer Institute working paper
data: Survey of ~100,000 workers across 11 exposed occupations linked to Danish matched employer-employee administrative registers
findings: Half of workers in exposed occupations had used ChatGPT, but women were 16 percentage points less likely than men to have used it for work, and adoption skewed toward younger, less experienced, higher-achieving, male workers. Employer restrictions and lack of training were cited as key barriers despite workers perceiving large productivity potential. Adoption had minimal short-run effects on wages or hours, with precisely estimated null effects of less than 2% two years after ChatGPT's release.
magnitude: Women 16pp less likely than men to use ChatGPT at work; wage/hours effects <2% after two years

findings: [India] Assam’s government embarked on a transformational journey using GovTech tools to overhaul its public finance management systems. By adopting digital platforms for budgeting, accounting, and procurement, Assam increased transparency and financial accountability across departments. The reforms are associated with improved service delivery and financial discipline.

Estimates the impacts of mobile broadband coverage on household welfare in Nigeria. The analysis exploits a unique data set that integrates a longitudinal household survey with information from Nigerian mobile operators on the deployment of mobile broadband internet between 2010 and 2016. Overall, estimates show that mobile broadband coverage had large and positive impacts on household consumption thereby reducing poverty significantly. 3/4G coverage results in a statistically significant increase in total consumption by 10.8 percent, consisting of an increase in food consumption by 10.2 percent and non-food consumption by 11.7 percent. This effect is if anything stronger among poorer households. Labor force participation explains a big part of this welfare-enhancing effect.

Study the short- and long-term effects of a large-scale state-sponsored program in India that aimed to close digital gender gaps by transferring free smartphones to women while constructing 4G towers to bring rural areas online. The paper uses an event study design to study the short-term impact, drawing on survey data collected in the capital district a few weeks before and after phone distribution. To investigate long-term effects, the paper uses a regression discontinuity approach, utilizing primary statewide survey data collected nearly five years after the program concluded. The program was well implemented, reversing gender gaps in smartphone ownership in the short run. However, many women lost ownership and gender gaps in use quickly worsened as men made use of the new phones. Nearly 5 years after the program began, there is limited evidence of persistent effects across a range of outcomes, including phone ownership and use, gender norms, access to information, and local economic activity, although there is some evidence of sectoral reallocation in the labor market. Despite widespread increase in smartphone adoption across households, digital gender gaps persist and were not affected by the program. Our findings suggest that in gender-unequal, resource-constrained settings, addressing affordability alone may not close digital gender gaps.

design: Firm-level panel analysis of cloud service adoption and long-run size growth rates
title: Scaling up to the cloud: Cloud technology use and growth rates in small and large firms
data: French firm-level panel data on cloud service adoption and firm size/growth
findings: Cloud service adoption positively affects the long-run size growth rate of French firms, with smaller firms benefiting substantially more than larger firms. The authors interpret this as evidence that cloud technologies reduce barriers to digitalization that disproportionately constrain smaller enterprises, in contrast to much of the broader ICT literature where technology adoption tends to favor larger incumbents.
magnitude: Cloud adoption raises long-run firm growth rates in France, with smaller firms gaining disproportionately more than larger firms

findings: Randomized the placement of mobile towers enabling use of mobile phones across rural locations in the Philippines. The share of households in treated villages increased the probability of placing a call by 0.416 standard deviations. Annual household income for treated households increased by 17 percent relative to control group, household expenditure over the last week increased by 10 percent, income earned per household member while away over the last year increased by 43 percent. The benefits are especially large for self-employed and those who migrate for work.

Analyze the adoption of AI by U.S. firms using data from the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS) covering September 2023 to February 2024. They find that an increase in AI usage from 3.7% to 5.4% among firms. AI adoption is higher in large firms and sectors like information, which reports an 18.1% usage rate. Common AI applications include marketing automation, virtual agents, and data analytics. Notably, firms using AI reported better overall performance and higher employment growth.

Examine the impact of IT capabilities on productivity and innovation, noting traditional IT measures are outdated. They create new IT metrics based on demands for IT skills from 2010 to 2022. These metrics correlate strongly with official productivity measures, showing that a 1% increase in IT skills results in a 0.009% sales increase ($540,000). These metrics are positively associated with firm innovation, measured by the number of patents, citations, and the real value of patents.

Carlana and La Ferrara (2024) study the Tutoring Online Program (TOP), where: (i) tutoring is entirely online; (ii) tutors are volunteer university students, matched with underprivileged middle school students. The paper leverages random assignment to estimate effects during and after the pandemic (2020 and 2022), investigating channels of impact. Three hours of individual tutoring per week increased math performance by 0.23 SD in 2020 and 0.20 SD in 2022. Higher-dosage yielded stronger effects, while group tutoring smaller effects. TOP enhanced students’ aspirations, socio-emotional skills and psychological well-being, but only during school closures. We also estimate the impact of TOP on tutors, finding increases in empathy.

authors: Compute energy and water demand estimates
findings: The insatiable energy and cooling demand from compute can strain existing energy and water infrastructure and exacerbate environmental impacts if not managed properly. Training GPT-4 consumed 52,000 Megawatt hour of electricity, an amount that can power an average US home for 5,200 years. It is estimated that a single ChatGPT query consumes 15 times more energy than a Google search query. An International Energy Agency (IEA) report found that data centers consumed 460TWh electricity in 2022, a figure that could exceed 1,000 TWh by 2026. At present, data centers worldwide consume 1-2% of overall power, but this percentage will likely rise to 3-4% by the end of the decade. Along the way, the carbon dioxide emissions of data centers may more than double between 2022 and 2030. The training and application of these massive AI models also generates prodigious heat output that pose cooling challenges. A lot of water is used in cooling for the servers that run AI applications. Half a liter of water evaporates for each ChatGPT conversation of about 29-50 queries. As these generative AI tools are used billions of times every month, the water usage quickly adds up to enormous sums.

design: Task-based macro model calibrated via Hulten's theorem
title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
data: Calibration combining existing task-exposure estimates (e.g., Eloundou et al.) and task-level productivity/cost-saving estimates (e.g., Noy & Zhang) within a task-based aggregation framework
findings: Evaluates the macroeconomic implications of advances in AI. Using existing estimates on exposure to AI and productivity improvements at the task level, the macroeconomic effects of AI appear nontrivial but modest, with a GDP growth between 0.9-1.6% and no more than a 0.71% increase in total factor productivity over 10 years. The paper then argues that even these estimates could be exaggerated, because early evidence is from easy-to-learn tasks, whereas some of the future effects will come from hard-to-learn tasks, where there are many context-dependent factors affecting decision-making and no objective outcome measures from which to learn successful performance. Consequently, predicted TFP gains over the next 10 years are even more modest and are predicted to be less than 0.55%. The paper also explores AI's wage and inequality effects. It shows theoretically that even when AI improves the productivity of low-skill workers in certain tasks (without creating new tasks for them), this may increase rather than reduce inequality. Empirically, the paper finds that AI advances are unlikely to increase inequality as much as previous automation technologies because their impact is more equally distributed across demographic groups, but there is also no evidence that AI will reduce labor income inequality. AI is also predicted to widen the gap between capital and labor income.
magnitude: Aggregate TFP gains capped at ≤0.66% over 10 years

findings: Some reports have found that large data centers use five million gallons of water per day, equivalent to the water use of a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. And U.S. data centers consumed 183 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, roughly 4% of the country’s total electricity consumption and approximately equal to the annual electricity demand of Pakistan. By 2030, that consumption is expected to more than double.

design: Conceptual/perspective essay synthesizing evidence on expertise and AI capability
title: Applying AI to Rebuild Middle Class Jobs
data: No new empirical dataset; synthesizes evidence on expert decision-making tasks and AI capabilities
findings: Argues that unlike earlier computerization, which favored elite experts and hollowed out middle-skill jobs, AI could extend the reach of non-elite workers into high-stakes expert decision-making tasks (medical care, document production, coding, teaching), potentially rebuilding middle-class job opportunities. Emphasizes this outcome depends on deliberate policy and firm choices to direct AI toward complementing rather than merely replacing workers.
magnitude: Conceptual framework: no single quantitative estimate; central claim is AI's potential to extend expert-level decision-making to non-elite workers

design: Historical job-title and patent-text analysis linked to Census occupational records, 1940-2018
authors: David Autor, Caroline Chin, Anna Salomons, Bryan Seegmiller
title: New Frontiers: The Origins and Content of New Work, 1940-2018
venue: Quarterly Journal of Economics (NBER Working Paper 30389)
data: Eight decades of new job-title data linked to US Census occupational records and patent texts distinguishing labor-augmenting from labor-automating innovation
findings: The majority of current US employment is in job specialties created after 1940. The locus of 'new work' shifted from middle-paid production/clerical jobs (1940-1980) to high-paid professional work and, secondarily, low-paid services (since 1980). New work emerges from augmenting innovations and rising occupational demand, while automating innovations suppress it; the demand-eroding effect of automation has intensified over the last four decades while the offsetting effect of augmentation has not kept pace.
magnitude: Majority of current US employment sits in post-1940 'new work'; automation's demand-eroding effect has outpaced augmentation's offsetting effect since 1980

findings: Demirer et al. 2024 study how firms respond to privacy laws in the context of the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) by using seven years of confidential data from one of the world’s largest cloud-computing providers. The difference-in-difference estimates indicate that, in response to the GDPR, EU firms decreased data storage by 26% and processing by 15% relative to comparable US firms, becoming less “data-intensive.” To estimate the costs of the GDPR for production, the authors propose and estimate an “information” production function framework where data and computation serve as inputs to production. The paper finds that data and computation are strong complements in production and that firm responses are consistent with the GDPR representing a 20% increase in the cost of data on average, with smaller firms bearing higher cost increases than larger ones. The production cost of information increased by 4% on average, with higher costs in more data-intensive industries.

Studies the causal impact of GenAI on writers’ creativity. It finds that access to GenAI causes stories to be more creative, better written, and more enjoyable, especially among less creative writers. However, GenAI-enabled stories are more similar to each other than stories by humans alone. These results point to an increase in individual creativity at the risk of losing collective novelty. This dynamic resembles a social dilemma: with GenAI, individual writers are better off, but collectively a narrower scope of novel content may be produced.

Studies the role of technology to improve tax capacity in the developing world. They focus on local property taxation in Ghana, a potentially significant but under-collected source of revenue. The paper randomizes the use of a new technology designed to help revenue collectors locate property owners to deliver tax bills, which is a major challenge in many developing countries with incomplete property addressing. The paper finds that the technology increases bill deliveries by 27 percent and, surprisingly, increases tax collections by 103 percent.

Examined the relationship between mobile broadband intensity and CO2 emissions using data from 181 countries between 2002 and 2020. Utilizing a difference-in-difference specification and an instrumental variable approach, the study found that while the initial introduction of mobile broadband is associated with an increase in CO2 emissions due to infrastructure investments and increased electricity consumption, a 10-percentage point increase in mobile broadband penetration leads to a 7% reduction in CO2 emissions per capita over time. This effect is significant only in high-income countries where mobile broadband penetration and speeds are higher.

Goldbeck & Lindlacher (2024, unpublished) use variation in submarine cable arrival timing to show evidence of large effects of internet penetration on economic growth and productivity in Sub-Saharan Africa.

In China, the mountainous province of Guizhou in Southwest has become a pioneer in China’s big data industry. Guizhou has 37 big data centers in operation or under construction as of early 2023, one of the cities with the biggest number of super large data centers globally. Data center investments have powered Guizhou’s digital economy development, achieving top growth rate in China for seven consecutive years since it became the big data pilot area in 2016. Data center investments also transformed the province’s industry structure. The software and ICT service sector’s contribution to local economic growth reached 45% in 2022 in Gui’an New Area and Guiyang, where the data centers are concentrated in.

Provides an overview of existing evidence from 150 studies on the extent to which, and how, internet connectivity affects economic development. Not surprisingly, estimates vary widely with the context, particular outcome, and form of internet studied. Overall the literature points towards sizeable economic impacts in many—though not all—settings.

Gave a random subset of medium-sized Liberian firms vouchers for a week-long program targeting equal-opportunity access to the input purchases of government, companies, and other organizations—a market that makes up upwards of 80 percent of global GDP. The program exclusively teaches “sellership”: how to navigate large buyers’ complex, formal sourcing procedures. Firms that participate win three times as many formal contracts a year later. The impact is heterogeneous: informational sales barriers bind for about a quarter of Liberian firms. Three years post-training, these firms continue to win desirable contracts, are more likely to operate, and employ more workers.

Found that in Denmark, more than half of workers have used ChatGPT in May 2024, 40 percent have used it for work, 24 percent for a core job task. Adoption rates differ across occupations, with IT-prone and high-skilled occupations, such as software developers and marketing specialists, leading the curve with rates of adoption around 78%.15 Occupations with lower educational requirements and where employers may restrict usage, such as office clerks and financial advisors, have the lowest adoption rates, around 36%. Women are 18 percentage points less likely to use ChatGPT than comparable men in the same occupation, age, experience, and earnings levels.

Conducted a randomized control trial at the US Military Academy during the COVID-19 pandemic to compare online and in-person learning outcomes. The study finds that students in online sections experienced a 0.236 standard deviation decrease in final grades, which is approximately 1.65 percentage points lower than their in-person counterparts. The negative effects were most pronounced among students with below-median academic ability. Male students, those who attended preparatory school, and prior enlisted personnel showed larger learning deficits in the online format. The study attributes the decline in performance to reduced student engagement, concentration difficulties, and weaker student-instructor relationships.

design: Nationally representative firm survey (Census Annual Business Survey)
authors: Kristina McElheran, J. Frank Li, Erik Brynjolfsson, Zachary Kroff, Emin Dinlersoz, Lucia Foster, Nikolas Zolas
title: AI Adoption in America: Who, What, and Where
venue: Journal of Economics & Management Strategy (NBER Working Paper 31788)
data: 2018 Annual Business Survey (Census Bureau/NCSES), ~850,000 US firms, covering five AI technologies (machine learning, NLP, machine vision, voice recognition, automated-guided vehicles)
findings: Fewer than 6% of US firms used any measured AI technology in 2018, but weighted by employment, average adoption was just over 18%, since most very large firms report some AI use. Adoption clusters in superstar tech hubs and among younger, VC-backed, highly-educated-founder firms with recent product/process innovation, raising concerns about a widening 'AI divide' across firms and regions.
magnitude: <6% of firms use AI (unweighted) vs ~18% employment-weighted adoption (2018)

findings: Unveils the real-time usage patterns of generative AI tools by individuals across countries. As of March 2024, the top 40 generative artificial intelligence tools attract nearly 3 billion visits per month from hundreds of millions of users. Generative artificial intelligence users skew young, highly educated, and male, particularly for video generation tools, with usage patterns strongly indicating productivity-related activities. Middle-income economies have disproportionately high adoption of generative AI relative to their economic scale, accounting for over 50% of GenAI global traffic. Income level, share of youth population, digital infrastructure, specialization in high-skill tradable services, English proficiency, and human capital contribute to higher generative AI uptake. The paper also documents disruptions in online traffic patterns and emphasizes the need for targeted investments in digital infrastructure and skills development to harness the full potential of artificial intelligence.

Employ a Structural Equation Modelling to analyze the relationship between ICT development (digital skills being a part of ICT development) and GDP growth using data from the Digital Economy and Society Index, EUROSTAT, and OECD between 2017 to 2022. They find a positive correlation between ICT advancements and GDP growth, highlighting the significant role of human capital (digital skills as a part of human capital, includes basic and advanced digital competencies necessary for effective ICT utilization), e-government, and the integration of digital technology as key factors. The study reports a path coefficient of 0.361, indicating a statistically significant positive relationship.

design: Occupational transition-matrix analysis by AI exposure/complementarity category
authors: Mauro Cazzaniga, Carlo Pizzinelli, Emma Rockall, Marina Mendes Tavares
title: Exposure to Artificial Intelligence and Occupational Mobility: A Cross-Country Analysis
data: Worker-level occupational transition histories in Brazil and the UK, classified by AI exposure and human-AI complementarity
findings: In both Brazil and the UK, college-educated workers frequently transition from high-exposure/low-complementarity occupations into high-exposure/high-complementarity occupations, a pattern especially common among young college-educated workers and associated with wage gains. The authors warn AI-driven structural change could simultaneously expand career-progression opportunities for some young workers while disrupting others by removing traditional stepping-stone jobs.
magnitude: Young college-educated workers disproportionately move from low- to high-complementarity AI-exposed jobs, with associated wage gains

design: Cross-country occupational AI-exposure/complementarity index applied to national employment structures
authors: Mauro Cazzaniga, Florence Jaumotte, Longji Li, Giovanni Melina, Augustus J.
title: Gen-AI: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work
countries: Advanced, emerging market, and low-income economies
data: Occupation-level AI exposure/complementarity index applied to employment structures across advanced, emerging, and low-income economies
findings: Almost 40% of global employment is exposed to AI, but exposure is highly unequal: about 60% of jobs are exposed in advanced economies (roughly half likely to benefit from complementarity, half at risk of displacement or wage decline), versus 40% in emerging markets and 26% in low-income countries. Women and college-educated workers are more exposed on average but also better positioned to benefit; inequality could rise if AI strongly complements high earners and capital returns increase.
magnitude: 40% of global employment exposed to AI; 60% in advanced economies vs 26% in low-income countries

findings: Investigates how the arrival of high-speed internet in Africa triggered FDI into the region. It also explores the role of complementary infrastructure, such as access to electricity and road connectivity, in amplifying the impact of internet connectivity on investment. To causally estimate impacts, the paper exploits plausibly exogenous variations in access to high-speed internet induced by the staggered arrival of submarine fiber-optic internet cables and spatial variations in terrestrial fiber cable networks across locations on the continent. Findings from the paper indicate that access to high-speed internet induces FDI, the probability of receiving FDI increases by about 6.3 percentage points. Also, the arrival of high-speed internet is associated with an increase in the number and size of FDI receipts by 10.5 percent and 33.4 percent, particularly in the service sector, with the finance, technology, retail, and health services subsectors as the main beneficiaries. Access to (hard) infrastructure, such as electricity and roads, amplifies the impact of internet connectivity on FDI, thus highlighting the role of complementarities in the impact of infrastructure. Further, the results suggest that improvement in quality of governance and increased performance of incumbent firms are plausible mechanisms.

authors: MIT Press Reader / data-center energy estimate
findings: Cloud data centers, essential for modern digital infrastructure, are energy-intensive, A single data center can consume the equivalent electricity of 50,000 homes and producing a greater carbon footprint than the airline industry. (Source: MIT Press)

Moritz Moller et al. (2024) present first evidence that generative AI can increase the speed of learning substantially in university students. The paper tested whether using the AI-powered teaching assistant Syntea affected the speed of learning of hundreds of distance learning students across more than 40 courses at the IU International University of Applied Sciences. The analysis suggests that using Syntea reduced their study time substantially—by about 27% on average—in the third month after the release of Syntea. Taken together, the magnitude of the effect and the scalability of the approach implicate generative AI as a key lever to significantly improve and accelerate learning by personalization.

design: Randomized field experiment (GPT-4 WhatsApp business mentor vs. standard guide control)
authors: Nicholas Otis, Rowan Clarke, Solène Delecourt, David Holtz, Rembrand Koning
title: The Uneven Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Entrepreneurial Performance: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Kenya
data: 640 Kenyan micro/small business owners randomized to a standard business guide (control) or a GPT-4-powered AI business mentor delivered via WhatsApp
findings: AI access raised revenue and profit by about 15% for high-performing entrepreneurs but reduced them by nearly 10% for previously low-performing entrepreneurs. The divergence was driven not by differences in the AI advice received but by which advice entrepreneurs chose to seek and implement: low performers tended to ask AI about more difficult, less tractable business problems.
magnitude: +15% revenue/profit for high performers vs approximately -10% for low performers

findings: [Nigeria] pioneered the use of digital platforms to foster participatory budgeting and project monitoring, enhancing trust between citizens and the government. Through initiatives like the Eyes and Ears App and the Citizens Feedback Platform, residents could report issues and suggest improvements.

Data centers can drive local economic development, create jobs, catalyze structural transformation, and boost tax revenues. Northen Virginia, the densely populated suburbs located just outside the US capital, is home to 70% of the world’s data centers. A government report in 2020 estimated that the data center industry in Virginia created nearly 15,000 direct jobs with an average annual pay of US$126,000, US$1.9 billion in associated pay and benefits, and $4.5 billion in economic output in 2018 alone. Taking into account the economic ripple effects generated by direct investment generated, the job creation amounts to more than 45,000, with US$3.5 billion in associated pay and benefits, and US$10.1 billion in economic output. Moreover, data centers generated US$600.1 million in state and local tax revenue. Each direct job in the data center industry helps to create 7.4 indirect jobs on average throughout the US economy.

design: Cross-country occupation-level panel using an AIOE-style exposure measure
title: Artificial Intelligence and Wage Inequality
data: Occupation-level wage and AI-exposure panel for 19 OECD countries, 2014-2018, using a Felten-Raj-Seamans-style exposure measure
findings: No evidence that AI affected wage inequality between occupations over 2014-2018. However, within-occupation wage inequality declined more in occupations most exposed to AI (e.g., business, legal, and science/engineering professionals, managers), consistent with AI narrowing productivity differences between higher- and lower-performing workers doing the same job.
magnitude: No between-occupation wage-inequality effect 2014-18; within-occupation inequality fell more in high-AI-exposure occupations

design: Cross-country panel regression of cloud adoption and broadband penetration on sectoral economic outcomes across OECD countries (AWS-funded study)
title: Economic spillovers from cloud computing: evidence from OECD countries
venue: Information Technology for Development, Vol. 30(1), pp. 173-194
data: Cross-country panel of cloud adoption rates, broadband penetration, and sectoral GDP contribution across OECD countries
findings: Estimate the impact of cloud computing on economic performance. The paper uses a multi-equation model in which cloud computing is complementary with broadband to maximize the economic contribution of digital technologies. The paper found that for an average OECD country, an increase of 1% in firm cloud penetration will result in 0.31% increase in labor productivity, while the effect on TFP will range between 0.22% (TFP-FE) and 0.18% (TFP-OP). However, the impact of cloud computing depends on broadband penetration and cloud adoption, which, as expected, vary by country and industry. The sector benefitting from the largest economic impact is information and communications, followed by manufacturing, while in contrast, no impact was detected for the transportation sector.
magnitude: Cloud spillovers are largest in the information/communications sector, with OECD-wide cloud adoption surpassing 50% by 2024 (AWS-funded study)

design: Resume-based firm-level AI investment measure with instrumental-variables strategy
authors: Tania Babina, Anastassia Fedyk, Alex Xi He, James Hodson
title: Artificial Intelligence, Firm Growth, and Product Innovation
data: Novel firm-level AI investment measure built from ~535 million individual resumes (Cognism) and Burning Glass job postings (~180 million vacancies)
findings: AI-investing firms show a sharp rise in AI-related hiring across sectors and subsequently experience higher growth in sales, employment, and market valuation, driven primarily by increased product innovation. Results are robust to instrumenting AI investment with firms' historical exposure to universities' local supply of AI graduates; AI-driven growth concentrates among larger firms, consistent with rising industry concentration.
magnitude: AI investment linked to higher firm sales/employment/valuation growth via product innovation, concentrated among larger firms

findings: Data centers account for 1-1.5% of global electricity use. This high consumption contributes to increased greenhouse gas emissions from electricity generation, particularly if the energy sources are fossil fuels. The heat generated by servers requires substantial cooling, further increasing energy usage and emissions. Data centers, through their substantial energy use, are responsible for nearly 1% of energy related GHG emissions. (Source)

design: Human- and GPT-4-rated occupational task exposure rubric applied to the full US task inventory
authors: Tyna Eloundou, Sam Manning, Pamela Mishkin, Daniel Rock
title: GPTs are GPTs: Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models
data: Human annotators and GPT-4 rate O*NET task statements for exposure to LLMs and LLM-powered software across the full US occupational task inventory
findings: About 80% of the US workforce could have at least 10% of their work tasks affected by LLMs, and about 19% could see at least 50% of tasks affected. Roughly 15% of all US worker tasks could be completed as fast with equivalent quality using an LLM alone; incorporating LLM-powered software raises this to 47-56% of tasks. Exposure rises with wage and education level, unlike prior waves of automation.
magnitude: 19% of US workers have ≥50% of tasks exposed to LLMs; 47-56% of tasks completable with LLM-powered software

design: Differential industry-level exposure to cloud computing and AI infrastructure cost reductions in China
authors: Yao Lu, Gordon M. Phillips, Jia Yang
title: The Impact of Cloud Computing and AI on Industry Dynamics and Concentration
data: Chinese industry/firm-level data on differential cloud and AI adoption exposure
findings: Cloud computing adoption is associated with increased firm entry, exit, and likelihood of M&A, and decreases industry concentration; AI adoption, by contrast, has no effect on entry but reduces the likelihood of exit and M&A and increases industry concentration, with benefits concentrated among larger firms. Firms with greater cloud exposure increase equity and venture capital financing, while only large firms increase equity financing in response to AI exposure.
magnitude: Cloud computing decreases industry concentration while AI adoption increases it, a divergent effect on Chinese market structure

findings: Study the extent to which machine learning methods can accurately differentiate ultra-poor households eligible for program benefits from ineligible households. The paper shows that machine learning methods leveraging mobile phone data can identify ultra-poor households nearly as accurately as survey-based measures of consumption and wealth; and that combining survey-based measures with mobile phone data produces classifications more accurate than those based on a single data source.

Focuses on the impact of information technology on the lives and livelihoods of rural households in sub-Saharan Africa, where simple mobile phones have leapfrogged traditional communication and financial technologies, and thus, arguably, offer some of the greatest potential for development. Drawing on primary and secondary research from a variety of disciplines, the authors examine the evolution of mobile phone coverage and adoption in sub-Saharan Africa over the past two decades, before exploring the main channels through which mobile phones can affect development. They then review initiatives on “digitizing development” and evaluate empirical evidence on their impact. The book argues that digital has yet to live up to the hype, ending with a set of questions that stakeholders should ask (and answer) when using digital technology for promoting development.

Analyzed digital technology use among microenterprises in seven Sub-Saharan African countries during 2017-18. Firms using accounting software or inventory control systems are associated with a 1.6-person larger firm size. Female-owned firms use digital technologies significantly less. Men are 3.3 times more likely to use computers compared to females. Over 70% of non-users cite lack of need as the main constraint.

Analyze the creation of new job titles from 1940 to 2018 using negative binomial regression and instrumental variables models. They find that augmentation innovations significantly increase new job titles by approximately 2.4% per decade (per 10% increase in augmentation patenting exposure), while automation innovations show an insignificant impact. The elasticity of employment to augmentation was higher from 1940 to 1980 compared to 1980 to 2018, indicating a slowdown in new work creation in recent decades. The locus of new work creation has shifted from middle-paid production and clerical occupations (1940-1980) to high-paid professional and low-paid service occupations (1980-2018).

Applies a difference-in-differences estimation using panel household survey data combined with geospatial information on the rollout of mobile broadband coverage in Tanzania. The results reveal that being covered by 3G networks has a large positive effect on total household consumption and poverty reduction, driven by positive impacts on labor-market outcomes. Being covered by 3G is associated with a 7 percent increase in consumption, 6 percent increase in food consumption, and 9 percent increase in non-food consumption. Basic need poverty rate declines by 5 percentage points. 3G coverage is positively associated with a 3 percentage points increase in labor-force participation. Working-age individuals living in areas covered by mobile internet witnessed an increase in labor-force participation, wage employment, and non-farm self-employment, and a decline in farm employment. These effects vary by age, gender, and skill level. Younger and more skilled men benefit the most through higher labor-force participation and wage employment, while high-skilled women benefit from transitions from self-employed farm work into non-farm employment.

Compares how in-kind food assistance, and an electronic voucher-based program affect the delivery of aid in practice. The Government of Indonesia randomized across 105 districts the transition from in-kind rice to approximately equivalent electronic vouchers redeemable for rice and eggs at a network of private agents. Targeted households received 46 percent more assistance in voucher areas. For the bottom 15 percent of households at baseline, poverty fell 20 percent. Voucher recipients received higher-quality rice, and increased consumption of eggs. The results suggest moving from a manual in-kind to electronic voucher-based program reduced poverty through increased adherence to program design.

Evaluated the impact of eBay's Seller Hub on small businesses through a field experiment conducted from May 12 to August 8, 2016. Seller Hub helps sellers track performance metrics, such as sales, traffic, and feedback, enabling quick responses to market changes and improved service quality. The randomized rollout to eBay sellers showed that Seller Hub access increased weekly sales by 3.6% on average, with adopters seeing a 12.5% increase. Benefits included higher quantities sold, better feedback scores, more new listings, and improved inventory management, all without significant changes in average prices. Sellers who actively used performance metrics saw greater benefits.

Follow the introduction of mobile money for the first time in rural villages of Mozambique using a randomized field experiment. The paper finds that mobile money increased migration out of these villages, where lower agricultural activity and investment is observed. At the same time, remittances received and welfare of rural households increased, particularly when facing geo-referenced village-level floods and household-level idiosyncratic shocks. The paper suggests that mobile money can accelerate urbanization and structural change in Sub-Saharan Africa.

design: Instrumental variables — Bitcoin price movements instrument for local cryptomining electricity demand
title: When cryptomining comes to town: high electricity-use spillovers to the local economy
countries: United States (Upstate New York), with a comparative analysis for China
data: County electricity billing and load data, cryptomining facility locations, Bitcoin price series, local business and employment records
findings: Cryptomining's very large local electricity demand raises bills for everyone else on the same grid. Using Bitcoin price movements to instrument for mining activity, the paper finds that ratepayers in affected Upstate New York counties bore roughly $204 million in additional annual electricity costs for households and $92 million for small businesses. Increased local business tax revenue offset only part of this. In China, mining-related electricity rationing was associated with lower wages and reduced investment, indicating crowding out of other electricity users.
magnitude: $204 million extra annual household electricity costs and $92 million for small businesses in affected counties; tax gains offset only part of the burden

findings: Found that an initiative by the Afghan government to modernize its payroll system – requiring teachers to biometrically register and receive salary payments via mobile money – significantly reduced delays and improved educational outcomes and financial inclusion, but did not decrease payments to non-existent ghost workers.

Find that from 2018 to 2020, establishments with robots tend to be larger, with more employees and a higher share of production workers, while also exhibiting lower earnings per worker. The presence of robot integrators in a locality significantly increases the likelihood of that area being classified as a Robot Hub by 20-25 percentage points. The geographic concentration of robot adoption leads to localized spillover effects, impacting employment and productivity in those regions.

Make use of the high-lightening area IV approach and focus specifically on Rwanda between 2002 (with no mobile internet coverage) and 2019. They find that “improvements in the coverage of 3G mobile internet technologies increase the share of employed individuals, among whom are both skilled and unskilled workers, with the former increasing at a faster rate, given their relatively small initial size; sectoral shift employment towards services and, within the service sector, to some high value-added and skill-intensive industries. A 10 percentage point increase in 3G coverage increases the share of working age population that is employed by 3.4 percentage points. Education, migration, and shifts in demand are instrumental in explaining these findings. A 10 percentage point increase in 3G coverage increases the average years of schooling by 0.15 years.
